stats.line: 11% of Americans aged 18 to 24 vape, twice as many as smoke cigarettes (5.3%). 17% use some tobacco or nicotine product.
stats.mirror: Vapes every day, never smoked, doesn't call himself a smoker

basis.who: adults 18+, table row for ages 18 to 24
basis.measured: Current use = every day or some days. The quote is a table row; its columns: any tobacco 17.0%, combustible 8.5%, cigarettes 5.3%, cigars 3.1%, pipes 1.5%, e-cigarettes 11.0%. Men of all ages: 24.1% any tobacco.

stats.caveat: Nicotine pouches were not asked about, so the true share of young nicotine users is likely higher. 2021 data.

ref.cite: Cornelius ME, Loretan CG, Jamal A, et al. (2023). Tobacco product use among adults - United States, 2021. MMWR Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report.

stats.line: 68% of US smokers want to stop, and 55% tried in the past year. Only 7.4% had recently quit.
stats.mirror: Tried to quit this year and is back on them

basis.measured: Self-reported wish to quit, a quit attempt in the past year, recent quitting, and use of counseling or medication. Only 31.2% used counseling or medication when trying to quit.

stats.caveat: Cigarette smokers only; vapers and pouch users were not asked. One year's snapshot, not a lifetime.

ref.cite: Babb S, Malarcher A, Schauer G, Asman K, Jamal A (2017). Quitting smoking among adults - United States, 2000-2015. MMWR Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report.
ref.quote: During 2015, 68.0% of adult smokers wanted to stop smoking, 55.4% made a past-year quit attempt, 7.4% recently quit smoking

stats.line: Some teens lost control over smoking within 2 days of their first inhale. Half lost it while smoking just 7 cigarettes a month.
stats.mirror: Started with a few at parties, now can't go a day

basis.who: sixth-grade students; 217 of them inhaled cigarettes
basis.measured: First sign of lost control on the 10-question Hooked on Nicotine Checklist, and full ICD-10 dependence. 127 of 217 inhalers lost control; half of the 83 who became dependent did so by 46 cigarettes a month.

stats.caveat: One sign of lost control is not full addiction. Teens and cigarettes only; vapes were not studied. The abstract doesn't say if 10% means all inhalers.

ref.cite: DiFranza JR, Savageau JA, Fletcher K, et al. (2007). Symptoms of tobacco dependence after brief intermittent use: the Development and Assessment of Nicotine Dependence in Youth-2 study. Archives of Pediatrics & Adolescent Medicine.
ref.quote: 10% having done so within 2 days … half had lost autonomy by the time they were smoking 7 cigarettes per month

stats.line: About 2 in 3 people who smoke a first full cigarette become dependent on nicotine at some point. For alcohol it's under 1 in 4.
stats.mirror: Thought he'd only ever smoke socially

basis.design: national survey (NESARC, two waves), survival analysis
basis.who: adults who had ever smoked a full cigarette
basis.measured: Age at first full cigarette and age at first meeting DSM-IV nicotine dependence (3 of 7 signs in a year). Within the first year about 2.0% were hooked; within 10 years 15.6%.

stats.caveat: A projection from what adults recalled, mostly about cigarettes. 'Dependent' means 3 of 7 signs in a year, not necessarily a pack a day.

ref.cite: Lopez-Quintero C, Pérez de los Cobos J, Hasin DS, et al. (2011). Probability and predictors of transition from first use to dependence on nicotine, alcohol, cannabis, and cocaine: results of the NESARC. Drug and Alcohol Dependence.
ref.quote: Lifetime cumulative probability estimates indicated that 67.5% of nicotine users, 22.7% of alcohol users, 20.9% of cocaine users, and 8.9% of cannabis users would become dependent

stats.line: Smokers in England spend about £20.49 a week on cigarettes, £27.66 if they buy packs. Vapers spend about £6.30.
stats.mirror: Buys a pack every couple of days and never counts it

basis.design: monthly national survey (new sample each month)
basis.who: adults who smoked or used other nicotine products
basis.measured: Self-reported average weekly spend, adjusted for inflation. The authors put the gap between smokers and people using only vapes or NRT at about £670 a year.

stats.caveat: Averages from what people reported in England; your spend depends on how much you use and local prices.

ref.cite: Jackson SE, Tattan-Birch H, Shahab L, Brown J (2023). How has expenditure on nicotine products changed in a fast-evolving marketplace? A representative population survey in England, 2018-2022. Nicotine & Tobacco Research.
ref.quote: Smokers spent £20.49 [95% CI = 20.09-20.91] on cigarettes each week (£27.66 [26.84-28.50] … e-cigarette users spent £6.30 [5.99-6.55]

stats.line: Smokers got about 14 minutes less sleep a night, fell asleep slower and had less deep sleep. Ex-smokers slept like never-smokers.
stats.mirror: Has one before bed and wakes up tired

basis.design: sleep study within a large cohort (Sleep Heart Health Study)
basis.who: adults: 2,916 never, 2,705 former and 779 current smokers
basis.measured: One overnight sleep recording (polysomnography) each: time to fall asleep (5.4 minutes longer), total sleep, and time in each sleep stage.

stats.caveat: One night per person; it shows a link, not proof that smoking caused it. Vapes were not studied.

ref.cite: Zhang L, Samet J, Caffo B, Punjabi NM (2006). Cigarette smoking and nocturnal sleep architecture. American Journal of Epidemiology.
ref.quote: Compared with never smokers, current smokers had a longer initial sleep latency (5.4 minutes, 95% confidence interval (CI): 2.9, 7.9) and less total sleep time (14.0 minutes

stats.line: Men who smoke have about 1.5 times the odds of erection problems of non-smokers. Ex-smokers: about 1.3 times.
stats.mirror: Smokes and has had trouble in bed, blamed nerves

basis.design: meta-analysis of 8 observational studies (4 cohort, 4 case-control)
basis.who: men; ages not in fetched text
basis.measured: Odds of erectile dysfunction in current and former smokers against non-smokers, from the 4 cohort studies.

stats.caveat: Shows a link, not proof of cause. These are odds, not a simple 'X% more likely'. Ages and countries are not in the abstract.

ref.cite: Cao S, Yin X, Wang Y, Zhou H, Song F, Lu Z (2013). Smoking and risk of erectile dysfunction: systematic review of observational studies with meta-analysis. PLoS One.
ref.quote: Compared with non-smokers, the overall odd ratio of ED in prospective cohort studies was 1.51(95% CI: 1.34 to 1.71) for current smokers

stats.line: The best estimate: smokers make about 30 quit attempts, on average, before one sticks. Failing many times is normal.
stats.mirror: Has quit a hundred times and thinks he's the exception

basis.design: cohort followed up to 3 years, surveyed every 6 months
basis.who: adult smokers who tried to quit
basis.measured: Quit attempts and lasting quits during follow-up, turned into attempts-per-success with a life table. Other methods gave 6.1, 19.6 and 142.

stats.caveat: An average that depends on the method; many people quit in far fewer tries. Cigarette smokers only.

ref.cite: Chaiton M, Diemert L, Cohen JE, et al. (2016). Estimating the number of quit attempts it takes to quit smoking successfully in a longitudinal cohort of smokers. BMJ Open.
ref.quote: ranged from 6.1 under the assumptions consistent with prior research … 29.6 using the method with the expected lowest bias

stats.line: Only 3–5% of quit attempts made with no help last 6 to 12 months. Most slips happen in the first 8 days.
stats.mirror: Quits cold turkey on Monday, smoking again by the weekend

basis.design: systematic review (too few, too mixed studies to pool)
basis.who: smokers trying to quit without treatment
basis.n: a summary of 10 studies plus 2 studies and 3 no-treatment control groups; people not counted in fetched text
basis.measured: Share still not smoking 6 to 12 months after one quit attempt, and when relapse happens.

stats.caveat: This is per attempt, not per person: many people try again and succeed later.

ref.cite: Hughes JR, Keely J, Naud S (2004). Shape of the relapse curve and long-term abstinence among untreated smokers. Addiction.
ref.quote: 3-5% of self-quitters achieve prolonged abstinence for 6-12 month after a given quit attempt.

stats.line: With varenicline, people were about 2.3 times as likely to stay off cigarettes for 6+ months as with a dummy pill.
stats.mirror: Thinks quit pills are for weak people

basis.design: Cochrane review, 41 randomised trials for this comparison
basis.where: several countries (not listed in fetched text)
basis.measured: Not smoking at 6 months or longer, checked by breath or blood test where possible; varenicline against placebo.

stats.caveat: Prescription only; side effects are possible. Compared with a dummy pill. Mostly tested in cigarette smokers, not vapers.

ref.cite: Livingstone-Banks J, Fanshawe TR, Thomas KH, et al. (2023). Nicotine receptor partial agonists for smoking cessation. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews.
ref.quote: We found high-certainty evidence that varenicline helps more people to quit than placebo (RR 2.32, 95% CI 2.15 to 2.51; I2 = 60%, 41 studies, 17,395 participants)

stats.line: Patches, gum or lozenges make you about 1.5 times as likely to stay off cigarettes as quitting without them.
stats.mirror: Tried a patch once, didn't feel magic, gave up on it

basis.who: adults motivated to quit, mostly smoking 15+ cigarettes a day
basis.where: several countries (not listed in fetched text)
basis.measured: Not smoking after at least 6 months, any form of NRT against placebo or no NRT. Patch 1.64, gum 1.49.

stats.caveat: Compared with placebo or no NRT, in people who mostly smoked 15+ a day. Not tested here in vapers or pouch users.

ref.cite: Hartmann-Boyce J, Chepkin SC, Ye W, Bullen C, Lancaster T (2018). Nicotine replacement therapy versus control for smoking cessation. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews.
ref.quote: The RR of abstinence for any form of NRT relative to control was 1.55 (95% confidence interval (CI) 1.49 to 1.61).

stats.line: Quitters gain 4–5 kg on average in the first year, most of it in 3 months. About 1 in 6 lose weight.
stats.mirror: Afraid quitting will make him fat

basis.who: people who stayed quit in quit-smoking trials, with or without medication
basis.where: several countries (not listed in fetched text)
basis.measured: Weight change from quit day to 1, 2, 3, 6 and 12 months. At 12 months: 16% lost weight, 37% gained under 5 kg, 34% gained 5–10 kg, 13% gained over 10 kg.

stats.caveat: An average; it varies a lot between people. Measured in cigarette smokers in trials, not in vapers.

ref.cite: Aubin HJ, Farley A, Lycett D, Lahmek P, Aveyard P (2012). Weight gain in smokers after quitting cigarettes: meta-analysis. BMJ.
ref.quote: Smoking cessation is associated with a mean increase of 4-5 kg in body weight after 12 months of abstinence, and most weight gain occurs within three months of quitting.

stats.line: Among men with erection problems who quit smoking, at least 1 in 4 improved within a year. None who kept smoking did.
stats.mirror: Has erection trouble and smokes, never linked the two

basis.who: male smokers with erectile dysfunction and no other known cause, who asked for NRT
basis.measured: Erectile function score (IIEF-5) before and after one year.

stats.caveat: Small, not a trial. Older men and men with severe problems improved less.

ref.cite: Pourmand G, Alidaee MR, Rasuli S, Maleki A, Mehrsai A (2004). Do cigarette smokers with erectile dysfunction benefit from stopping?: a prospective study. BJU International.
ref.quote: After 1 year the ED status improved in > or = 25% of ex-smokers but in none of the current smokers

stats.line: People who quit smoking rated their life and mood better than those who kept smoking, at 1 year and at 3 years.
stats.mirror: Worried life will feel empty without cigarettes

basis.design: cohort within a randomised quit-smoking trial, followed 3 years
basis.where: US (site not named in fetched abstract)
basis.measured: Quality of life, health-related quality of life, mood, relationship satisfaction and stressful events; smoking checked by a biochemical test. Quitters also had fewer stressors by year 3.

stats.caveat: Quitters weren't chosen at random, so they may differ in other ways. Marriage satisfaction did not change.

ref.cite: Piper ME, Kenford S, Fiore MC, Baker TB (2012). Smoking cessation and quality of life: changes in life satisfaction over 3 years following a quit attempt. Annals of Behavioral Medicine.
ref.quote: Compared with continuing smokers, quitters showed improved global QOL, HR-QOL, and affect at years 1 and 3 and fewer stressors by year 3.

rejected.claim: Page number '×2.3 the odds of quitting with varenicline' (existing).
rejected.why: Number checks out, word does not: 2.32 is a risk ratio, not odds. Correct: 'about 2.3 times as likely to quit' (still off cigarettes at 6+ months).

rejected.claim: Share of young US adults who use nicotine pouches.
rejected.why: No official adult figure fetched: SAMHSA's NSDUH pages returned 403 and the CDC adult survey did not ask about pouches. Only a preprint (medRxiv) found. CDC youth figure: 2.4% of high school students (2024).

rejected.claim: 22.3% of US 18–25-year-olds vaped nicotine in the past month (NSDUH 2025).
rejected.why: Seen only in a search snippet; the SAMHSA PDF returned 403, so it was not fetched.

rejected.claim: Two-thirds to three-quarters of ex-smokers quit unaided.
rejected.why: Not fetched from a primary source. Used instead: only 31.2% of US smokers used counseling or medication when trying to quit (CDC, 2015).

rejected.claim: Nearly 9 in 10 adults who smoke daily first tried smoking by age 18.
rejected.why: On a CDC page (fetched), but it names no survey, year or sample, so the basis cannot be filled. Left out.

rejected.claim: Quitting lowers anxiety and depression (Cochrane 2021, 102 studies, 169,500 people).
rejected.why: Verified (Taylor 2021, PMID 33687070), but effects are standardised scores that don't turn into plain numbers; file 02 already has the 2014 version.

rejected.claim: A year after quitting, quitters report no significant craving (572 smokers).
rejected.why: Verified (Schlam 2012, PMID 22865499) but cut to stay at 14; no number to show.
